role_summary: Elite technical head of Turing's enterprise applied AI practice. This leader sets technical vision for applied GenAI systems, personally pressure-tests architecture, and partners with a senior business leader to shape how major BFSI enterprises deploy AI. The clearest positive signal is Executive Director or clearly ED-analogous scope: Head of AI or GenAI Engineering, Head of AI Platforms, Applied Science or Research leaders who translated research into deployed systems, principal architects, technology fellows, executive directors or equivalent senior builders at major financial institutions or BFSI-serving platforms, and hands-on startup CTOs who still read at that band. BFSI credibility is required for every viable path. Capital markets and institutional finance remain the highest-priority domain lanes after seniority, but broader BFSI workflows such as regulatory reporting, client onboarding, payments, insurance, wealth, and market infrastructure are still in-bounds. The real bar is exceptional technical depth, breadth, pedigree, and leadership stature rather than classic consulting-delivery tenure alone. GenAI evidence must be credible, but the question is whether the profile is a high-quality lead worth a conversation, not whether LinkedIn alone proves every architectural detail. Pure strategy, pure product, pure research-without-productization, and pure non-BFSI imports are out.
instructions: This market has already been worked repeatedly. The FIRST 8 strings should still prioritize hidden same-caliber populations over canonical big-bank cleanup pools or generic GenAI title searches.

Use the latest run as market intel, not just scorekeeping. The first 10-12 strings should still bias toward ED or ED-analogous technical leaders. Cover three lanes in parallel, but in this order: capital-markets and institutional-finance leaders first, broader BFSI technical leaders second, and BFSI-credible research-to-product or CTO-shaped transfers third.
BFSI credibility is a hard gate. No BFSI = no, even for elite technical, academic, or top-tech profiles.

Do not overfit to capital markets alone, but do keep capital markets and institutional finance as the primary domain lane once seniority is in range. Broader BFSI populations such as regulatory reporting, client onboarding, payments, insurance, wealth, custody, and market infrastructure are still in-bounds, but they should not crowd out capital-markets populations early.

Do not over-penalize research, science, or CTO-shaped profiles when BFSI credibility is real. Applied science managers, research leaders, chief AI architects, and startup CTOs are in-bounds when they clearly translated AI research into deployed systems, common platforms, or real teams AND also show clear BFSI or BFSI-serving workflow relevance.

Classic consulting or delivery tenure is a positive modifier, not a hard gate. Weight technical authority, architecture depth, executive presence, and platform-building more heavily than formal services pedigree.

Pedigree matters. Strong brand and authority signals such as Amazon, Bloomberg, Franklin Templeton, JPMorgan, Goldman, top market-infrastructure firms, advanced degrees, patents, publications, or recognized AI thought leadership should raise interest when paired with production-builder evidence.

Treat the brief's hints as semantic intent, not as a term checklist. Generate your own discriminative search vocabulary rather than echoing the hints verbatim, and prefer practitioner language, workflow language, product language, and hidden title variants over literal restatement.

Lead with technical-authority concepts as often as workflow concepts: shared AI platform ownership, common infrastructure used by multiple teams, research translated into deployed systems, senior technical stewardship below broad enterprise executives, and architecture-deep leadership rather than generic management.

Archetype-first executive-builder strings are valid openers, but keep them seniority-calibrated. ED, ED-analogous, Head, Principal Architect, Technology Fellow, Applied Science leader, and CTO strings should read at true lab-head scope, not just generic leadership.

Capital-markets workflow language still matters and should remain the strongest opening domain axis after seniority: research workflow, investment workflow, asset management, market data, post-trade, collateral, document intelligence, and institutional-finance operations remain the best pools.

Broader BFSI lanes such as payments, insurance, wealth, treasury, custody, and regulatory operations are secondary to capital markets, not co-equal opening focus areas. Use them only when the candidate still reads ED-analogous, technically elite, and clearly BFSI-credible.

Generate morphology-aware variants for every chosen anchor: singular and plural, hyphen and spaced variants, acronym plus expansion, and common practitioner shorthand. Missing lexical variants means missing candidates.

Evaluate for conversation-worthiness: ask whether this is a high-quality, conversation-worthy lead for the HM, not whether LinkedIn alone proves enough detail to hire the person today. Strong senior BFSI engineering leaders with specific high-level GenAI language can still be clean saves.

The evaluation bar stays extremely high: NYC, 15+ years, post-2022 applied GenAI evidence, clear senior technical leadership, and enough stature to partner with a C-level executive one step below the CEO. ED or clearly ED-analogous scope and BFSI credibility are core gates. Hidden transfer populations are acceptable only inside BFSI; looser technical standards or under-leveled profiles are not.

intake_notes: The public JD reads like a services-led Head of AI Technology, but actual hiring-manager calibration is broader and more elite. The first hard gate is seniority: Executive Director or clearly ED-analogous technical leadership. The second hard gate is BFSI credibility: no BFSI means no match, even for elite technical or academic profiles. Capital markets and institutional finance remain the strongest domain prior after seniority, but broader BFSI workflows such as regulatory reporting, client onboarding, payments, insurance, wealth, custody, and market infrastructure are still in-bounds. The active candidate set and prior offer behavior show that the real target is not only classic delivery operators; research-to-product leaders, chief-AI-architect shapes, startup CTOs, and elite enterprise platform builders can all fit if they read at the same level of stature AND show real BFSI or BFSI-serving workflow credibility. Traditional consulting or delivery tenure is a positive modifier, not a hard gate. The GenAI question is not whether LinkedIn alone proves enough detail to hire the person on the spot; it is whether the profile gives credible reason to believe this is a high-quality lead worth a conversation. Strong senior BFSI engineering leaders with specific, high-level GenAI workflow language should therefore save cleanly rather than be rejected for lacking tool-name detail. The real hard bar is: NYC, 15+ years, post-2022 applied GenAI evidence, clear senior technical leadership, and enough technical authority to partner with the C-level executive who sits between this role and the CEO.

The strongest candidates have not only led teams, but also created common platforms, technical standards, evaluation infrastructure, or reusable playbooks that shaped how others built AI.

depth_distinction.builder_definition: A builder for this role personally drives the technical design, implementation, or research-to-production translation of applied AI systems in BFSI settings or BFSI-serving platforms. They do not just bless the architecture, sponsor the program, or lead the team from a distance. At this seniority, public profiles are often compressed, so do not require IC-style tool-name detail when the profile already shows ED-level scope, strong BFSI credibility, and specific GenAI workflow language. What matters is credible technical ownership and the ability to reason from first principles about models, retrieval, orchestration, evaluation, governance, deployment, and operational tradeoffs. A fit usually reads like Executive Director at a major bank or clear ED-analogous scope elsewhere: Head of AI, Head of AI Platforms, Chief AI Architect, Applied Science or Research leader, Principal Architect, Technology Fellow, Director or Senior Director at a relevant tech or finance organization, or a hands-on startup CTO who can credibly steer a lab-level technical function while still pressure-testing the system details.
depth_distinction.user_definition: A user or adjacent profile talks about AI, adopts AI, sells AI, scopes AI, or manages builders without personally building the production system. This includes AI strategy leaders, product heads, compliance operators who use technology, cloud or AI-vendor pre-sales, transformation executives, vendor-tool rollout owners, and large-org practice leaders whose recent work is mostly organizational rather than technical.
depth_distinction.edge_case_guidance: RESEARCH OR SCIENCE LEADERS: Do not reject applied-science, research-manager, or chief-scientist-shaped profiles on title alone if they translated research into deployed systems, common platforms, or significant enterprise capability, but they still need to read ED-analogous in scope and they still need visible BFSI credibility. GENAI DETAIL CALIBRATION: Senior engineering leaders rarely describe their GenAI work with IC-level specificity. If a profile is already clearly ED-analogous, clearly BFSI, and uses specific high-level GenAI workflow language, do not reject merely because the profile omits tool names or architecture diagrams. CONSULTING OR DELIVERY TITLES: Do not reject titles like Technology Fellow, Solutions Architect, Consulting Engineer, Delivery Lead, or Senior Manager on title alone. These can hide real builder-leaders if the bullets show personal engineering authorship for BFSI systems. BANK TITLE CALIBRATION: Executive Director remains the anchor target at major banks. VP, Director, Head, or Research-Manager shapes can fit if the scope reads truly elite and lab-like, but do not relax seniority just because the technical signal is good. Managing Director, global head, and comparable top-of-house innovation-lab leadership are usually too senior unless the profile still reads unusually technical. TOP TECH OR ENTERPRISE AI LEADERS: Amazon, Bloomberg, and similar research-to-product AI leaders are valid only when they show platform ownership, applied AI leadership, enterprise-grade productization, ED-analogous leadership scope, and explicit BFSI credibility. STARTUP CTOS OR FOUNDERS: At startups under roughly 150 employees, CTOs and co-founders can fit if they are still hands-on and the product clearly serves financial institutions or automates real BFSI workflows. CAPITAL MARKETS: Still the single strongest domain prior after seniority, but broader BFSI remains in-bounds.

inferential_save_rules.description: Reserve INFERENTIAL_SAVE for truly sparse but promising BFSI profiles where the title and trajectory strongly suggest fit, yet the public bullets are too thin to support a normal SAVE. If a profile already shows clear ED-level scope, clear BFSI credibility, and specific GenAI workflow language, use SAVE rather than INFERENTIAL_SAVE.

Hands-on CTO, chief AI architect, or co-founder at a small fintech, regtech, market-data, payments, or insurance company, with visible BFSI credibility but thin public detail

non_fit_patterns.label: AI-vendor sales, solutions, or customer-engineering leadership
non_fit_patterns.description: Customer-facing solutions, field CTO, customer engineering, or architecture roles at cloud or AI vendors where the work is demos, solutioning, POCs, and technical sales support rather than personal authorship of enterprise AI systems.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Client-facing gravitas is relevant, but the role requires a senior builder who personally ships the system. Demoing and advising on platform capabilities is not the same as engineering a production BFSI AI deployment.

non_fit_patterns.label: AI strategy, transformation, or product leadership
non_fit_patterns.description: Profiles centered on AI transformation, roadmaps, product management, AI strategy, or executive operating models rather than hands-on engineering authorship.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: The role needs someone who can personally pressure-test and direct the technical system. Strategy or product leadership without builder evidence is insufficient.

non_fit_patterns.label: Vendor-tool adoption mistaken for AI building
non_fit_patterns.description: AI experience is limited to rolling out vendor copilots, enterprise chat tools, or off-the-shelf AI enablement programs rather than building custom systems.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Adopting GitHub Copilot, Devin, or packaged AI tools is not the same as designing and shipping production applied AI systems.
examples: Led AI enablement using vendor tools

non_fit_patterns.label: Classical finance ML or analytics without post-2022 GenAI
non_fit_patterns.description: Strong quantitative, fraud, scoring, forecasting, or analytics profiles in finance without evidence of post-2022 applied GenAI delivery or architecture ownership.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: The domain is relevant, but the daily work is wrong. This role requires current applied GenAI builder depth, not just classical finance ML.

non_fit_patterns.label: Compliance, risk, or surveillance operators without builder evidence
non_fit_patterns.description: GRC, compliance-tech, risk-ops, surveillance, or regulatory-reporting profiles that use technology, run programs, or tune rules but do not personally architect and ship the AI system.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: The domain is adjacent, but the role needs a builder who can design and deliver the technical system, not an operator or oversight owner.

non_fit_patterns.label: Pure research or academic profiles without production delivery
non_fit_patterns.description: PhD, NLP, quant, or applied-science profiles where the visible signal is publications, patents, and research prestige but not productization, enterprise deployment, or technical leadership beyond the lab.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Research depth is welcome, but this role still requires applied system ownership, enterprise productization, or senior technical leadership beyond pure research output.

non_fit_patterns.label: Too-senior large-org AI or data leadership
non_fit_patterns.description: SVP, EVP, MD, CDAO, CIO, CTO of a very large engineering org, or Partner running a large AI practice where the recent work is organizational leadership rather than technical authorship.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Scope and compensation are usually wrong, and the profile is too far from hands-on system building for this role's bar.

non_fit_override_rule: Non-fit patterns describe default expectations for noisy populations, not absolute bans. Specific evidence that the candidate personally built and shipped production GenAI systems with strong BFSI workflow credibility overrides the non-fit pattern. This is especially important for consulting, architecture, science, founder, and adjacent executive-builder titles, which can hide real fits as easily as they can hide noise.

employer_signal_rules.evidence_required: BFSI institution alone is not enough. Save only when the profile clearly shows builder evidence in GenAI or applied AI systems and credible ownership of a consequential domain workflow. Executive Director remains the clearest target signal at major banks. VP, Director, Head, or research-manager shapes can also fit, but only if the scope reads clearly ED-analogous. Managing Director, global head, SVP, EVP, CDAO, CIO, or very large-org CTO is usually too senior unless the profile still reads unusually technical.
These employers are strong supportive signals for capital-markets, document-intelligence, and BFSI workflow credibility, but still require explicit builder evidence in applied AI or GenAI systems.

These employers are strong pedigree and technical-authority signals, especially for research-to-product AI leaders. Save only when the profile also shows clear ED-analogous senior leadership, enterprise or production system ownership, and visible BFSI credibility. No BFSI means no save. Pure research without productization is still not enough.

Insurance carriers are supportive signals when the profile clearly shows builder authorship in underwriting, claims, policy ops, actuarial, or insurance-risk workflows. Carrier logo alone is not enough.

Payments infrastructure employers are useful because they often hide candidates with large-scale, regulated workflow experience. Save only when the profile clearly shows production AI builder evidence tied to payments, transaction intelligence, fraud, or transaction-banking workflows.

Only save when the profile clearly shows build-and-deploy work for BFSI clients. Advisory, staffing, transformation, product, and partner-level roles are common false positives. Technology fellow, principal architect, engineering director, and consulting-engineering profiles can be excellent fits when the builder evidence is real.

Small startups under roughly 150 employees building institutional-finance, payments, insurance, regtech, market-data, or other BFSI systems are strong fits. Capital markets and institutional finance are still the single strongest prior, but startup CTOs and co-founders can fit only if they remain hands-on, the scope clearly maps to the target seniority band, and the profile shows real BFSI credibility.

Apply the same technical and leadership standard as any other candidate. Lesser-known employers can absolutely be strong fits if the actual enterprise workflow, applied AI work, and technical-authority signal are right.

minimum_bar_description: Fifteen or more years is a hard floor because the role must hit the ground running as the technical leader of an applied AI lab serving senior enterprise stakeholders and partnering closely with a C-level executive. Seniority and BFSI credibility are binary gates: the candidate must read Executive Director or clearly ED-analogous, and they must show real BFSI or BFSI-serving workflow credibility. Capital markets and institutional finance are the strongest domain signals after seniority, but broader BFSI workflows can still qualify. GenAI evidence is also required, but public detail will vary. The right standard is not whether LinkedIn alone proves enough detail to hire the person immediately; it is whether the profile gives credible reason to believe this is a high-quality lead worth a conversation. Strong senior BFSI engineering leaders with specific high-level GenAI workflow language should not be rejected merely because they do not enumerate tools, frameworks, or architecture choices. Head of AI, Head of AI Platforms, Chief AI Architect, Applied Science or Research leader, Principal Architect, Technology Fellow, VP Engineering, or hands-on startup CTO shapes can fit only when the actual scope maps to the target band and BFSI credibility is real. Traditional consulting or delivery-practice tenure helps but is not mandatory. Pure research without productization remains out. Major-bank Managing Director, global-head, and similarly broad executive profiles are usually above scope unless they still read unusually technical. Current NYC metro location is non-negotiable. Post-2022 GenAI work is required.
